acceptable.choice: Build it inside the existing Rails monolith as a namespaced admin area (e.g. Admin:: controllers, a separate layout, and its own routes constraint)
acceptable.why: The data is already in the app's Postgres, the team knows Rails well, and this is the fastest route with no new service to deploy or be on call for.

acceptable.choice: Hand-rolled Rails views with Hotwire/Turbo, plus Chartkick and groupdate for the usage-over-time charts
acceptable.why: Uses tools the team already knows, gives full control over the customer-success workflow, and adds only small, well-known gems.

acceptable.choice: An admin framework gem inside the monolith (ActiveAdmin, Administrate, Avo, or whichever one is already in the app)
acceptable.why: Gives search, filtering, and CSV export for internal users with little code; best if one is already installed, but heavy customization can make it fight back.

acceptable.choice: CSV export as a Sidekiq job that streams rows (find_each or Postgres COPY) to S3 and returns a presigned URL or an in-app or emailed link
acceptable.why: Keeps long exports out of Puma request threads and away from ALB timeouts, using job infrastructure they already run.

acceptable.choice: Streaming small CSVs straight from the controller (send_data or an Enumerator response) with a hard row cap
acceptable.why: Fine for small, bounded exports, as long as anything large goes through the background job path.

acceptable.choice: Account search with Postgres: indexed ILIKE, pg_trgm trigram indexes, or tsvector full-text search (e.g. the pg_search gem)
acceptable.why: Easily enough for 40 internal users and adds no new datastore.

acceptable.choice: Point the reporting queries at a Postgres read replica through Rails multi-database (connects_to / connected_to role: :reading)
acceptable.why: Keeps heavy aggregate and export queries off the primary that customers depend on, with little code and a small Terraform change if a replica doesn't exist yet.

acceptable.choice: Pre-aggregated usage rollup tables, or materialized views refreshed on a schedule by Sidekiq
acceptable.why: Keeps 'usage over time' queries cheap and predictable if the raw usage or event tables are large.

acceptable.choice: Run admin traffic as a separate ECS service from the same monolith image (its own target group or host rule)
acceptable.why: Optional isolation: admin load can't starve customer-facing web tasks, and there's still only one codebase and deploy pipeline.

acceptable.choice: An off-the-shelf internal BI or admin tool (Metabase, Retool) pointed at a read replica
acceptable.why: A reasonable alternative if CS mostly needs ad-hoc reporting, but it adds a service to run and a separate auth/PII surface, and it works around the app's domain logic rather than reusing it.

ruled_out.choice: A new standalone service (Go or Ruby) for admin reporting
ruled_out.why: Adds deploy, monitoring, and on-call load for a 40-user internal feature. It breaks their priorities of velocity and quiet on-call, and either duplicates domain logic or shares the database.

ruled_out.choice: Writing it in Go because the platform team knows Go
ruled_out.why: Only three people know Go and they use it for internal tooling. Product engineers are Rails people, so this creates a knowledge silo and pulls the platform team off platform work.

ruled_out.choice: A separate SPA (React/Next.js) with a new JSON API for the admin area
ruled_out.why: A second frontend stack and build/deploy pipeline is far more than server-rendered internal pages need, and it slows the Rails team down.

ruled_out.choice: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch for account search
ruled_out.why: A new stateful datastore plus sync logic and on-call burden, to solve a search problem Postgres handles at this scale.

ruled_out.choice: A data warehouse or CDC pipeline (Redshift, Snowflake, Kafka/Debezium) as the starting point
ruled_out.why: Heavy infrastructure and operations cost with no demonstrated need. Revisit only if reporting needs grow well beyond this feature.

ruled_out.choice: A separate app that connects directly to the monolith's Postgres schema
ruled_out.why: Shared-database coupling: schema migrations in the monolith can silently break it, and it skips the model-layer logic and authorization.

ruled_out.choice: Generating large CSVs synchronously in the web request with no limits
ruled_out.why: Ties up Puma threads, risks ALB/Fargate timeouts and memory spikes, and can hurt customer traffic. That's bad for a quiet on-call.

must_mention: The direct answer: no strong reason against it. Build it in the monolith, because the data, skills, deploy pipeline, and auth are already there and the audience is small and internal.
Exports must not run as long synchronous requests: use a background job (Sidekiq) to write the file to S3 or similar, then hand back a link, or cap the export size.
Protect the primary database: check query plans and add indexes, and consider a read replica and/or pre-aggregated rollups for usage-over-time queries, so reporting can't slow customer traffic.
Authentication and authorization for the admin area: staff-only access (ideally SSO), role checks (e.g. Pundit policies or an admin-only constraint), kept separate from customer auth.

Treat export as a sensitive action: audit-log who exported what, scope the data to what customer success needs, and consider rate limits, because CSVs of customer usage data are a common PII leak path.
Keep the code modular inside the monolith (namespace, or a Rails engine / packwerk package if they already use one) so the admin area doesn't tangle with core product code.
Postgres is enough for account search at this scale; no search engine is needed.
red_flags: Recommending microservices, a new Go service, or a separate deployable as the default for a 40-user internal admin feature.
Adding new infrastructure (Elasticsearch, a warehouse, Kafka, a separate SPA stack) with no measured need.
Suggesting synchronous, unbounded CSV generation in the web request, or loading whole result sets into memory (e.g. .all.to_csv on large tables).
Ignoring the risk of heavy reporting queries against the production primary database.
Leaving out authorization, audit logging, or PII handling for an area that can search and export all customers' data.
Telling them to grant customer-success staff raw SQL or database console access as the 'reporting' solution.
Framing the monolith itself as the problem (e.g. 'this is a good chance to start breaking up the monolith') when the stated goal is keeping it healthy and moving fast.
Missing CSV/formula injection when exporting customer-controlled strings that will be opened in Excel (escape leading =, +, -, @).
unknowns: How big the usage data is (row counts, raw events vs. already aggregated) and how expensive the over-time queries are on current data. This decides whether rollups or a replica are needed.
Typical and maximum export size (hundreds of rows vs. millions), which decides between streaming inline and a background job to S3.
Whether a Postgres read replica already exists, and whether its replication lag is acceptable for CS reporting.
Whether the app already has an admin framework, staff-auth/SSO setup, or modularity tooling (engines, packwerk) to reuse.
Compliance requirements (SOC 2, GDPR, customer contracts) for who can export customer data and what must be audited.
How fresh the usage data must be (real-time vs. daily), which affects whether materialized views or rollups are acceptable.
Whether customer success's needs are stable and well defined (favoring a purpose-built in-app page) or exploratory and ad hoc (where Metabase or Retool might fit better).
